# Order related work and make later results discoverable

[← All question groups](../index.md) · `messaging-ordering-correlation` · **Messaging & Event-Driven Systems** · Catalog level: senior

<p>Questions come from the preserved source notes. Reframing, assessment intent, senior signals and rubrics are editorial interpretations, not verified model answers or universal interviewer expectations. Follow-ups and the combined production exercise are agent additions. Reading this bank creates no learning record, score, completion or review schedule.</p>

## Start with one representative question

[S04-Q028](#S04-Q028)

<p>If work is accepted asynchronously, how would the caller receive or find its eventual result? Explain the contract for progress, completion and failure.</p>

## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Define how related asynchronous operations are ordered and how a caller can determine their outcomes.</p>

<ul>
<li>Distinguish message identity, correlation and direct causation.</li>
<li>Design caller-visible acceptance, progress and completion contracts.</li>
<li>Choose an ordering boundary while explaining slow-item and throughput consequences.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

- [Delivery contracts and recovery ownership](messaging-delivery-recovery.md)

<p>First identify how work is related and what caused it. Use that identity model to connect a submission to its result, then decide which operations really need a sequence. Ordering is useful only when it serves the business contract rather than obscuring unrelated parallel work.</p>

### S04-Q029 · Foundation

<p>What do correlation and causation identifiers represent in a message workflow? Trace both identifiers through a request that produces more than one event.</p>

**Source:** [S04-Q029](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q029)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S04-Q029](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q029)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain correlation and causation identifiers.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>One workflow can contain related events and direct triggering links. Explain which relationship each identifier records rather than assuming one identifier serves both purposes.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Distinguish investigation context from direct causal relationships.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Choose a generic workflow and establish naming conventions. Keep message identity, business-operation identity and trace context distinct.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Use a branching example to explain the two relationships.</li>
<li>Show how identifiers help investigate a failure without treating them as a deduplication guarantee.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Using one identifier for every purpose without defining its meaning.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What should be recorded when one message causes two different events?</li>
<li>Which identifier would you inspect to find the immediate trigger of a failed event?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S04-Q028"></a>

### S04-Q028 · Application

<p>If work is accepted asynchronously, how would the caller receive or find its eventual result? Explain the contract for progress, completion and failure.</p>

**Source:** [S04-Q028](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q028)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S04-Q028](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q028)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How would you return a result when communication is asynchronous?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Acceptance and completion are separate events. Follow one request from submission until the caller can determine its outcome.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Design an observable asynchronous result contract.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State caller capabilities, expected duration and who may read the result. Do not assume an HTTP response means the background operation has finished.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Connect submission identity to progress and the final outcome.</li>
<li>Handle a lost notification or disconnected caller with a verifiable recovery path.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Returning accepted and leaving the caller no way to learn whether work succeeded.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What should a repeated submission return while the original is running?</li>
<li>How do you prevent one caller from reading another caller&#x27;s result?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S04-Q027"></a>

### S04-Q027 · Trade-offs

<p>How would you decide the ordering boundary for messages while retaining useful throughput? Compare ordering all work with ordering only related work.</p>

**Source:** [S04-Q027](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q027)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S04-Q027](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q027)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What trade-off exists between ordering and throughput?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Ordering is about which operations must be observed in sequence. Explain the business dependency before deciding how much work may proceed in parallel.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Choose an ordering scope from correctness and capacity requirements.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Clarify whether order concerns delivery, processing start or committed effects. State broker/version and verify official guarantees, including failure and redelivery behavior.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Tie the required sequence to a specific business invariant.</li>
<li>Explain a slow-item or retry case and how to measure its throughput impact.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Claiming global order while processing messages concurrently without tracing completion order.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What should happen when an earlier operation is delayed?</li>
<li>How would you handle a message that arrives out of the required business sequence?</li>
</ul>

</details>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>A customer submits two updates for the same import job while another customer submits an unrelated job. Define the required ordering, identifiers and result-access contract. Trace a delayed first update, a disconnected client and an out-of-sequence completion; explain the trade-off for parallel workers and what you would observe.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Distinguishes identifier purposes and provides a way to find an asynchronous result.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Defines the exact ordering observation, protects related work and explains recovery and throughput limits with tests.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>A global-order claim or a result notification without sequence tests and lost-notification recovery does not establish the contract.</p>
